title: Predictably Irrational - basic human motivations:  Dan Ariely at TEDxMidwest
transcript: [Music] Okay. So, let's see. Um, I want to talk to you a little bit today about human motivation. What gets us to care and act and be active? And as a starting point, especially being in Chicago, close to the University of Chicago and economics department of Chicago, I think it's it's worthwhile to think that our basic idea about human motivation is that we think about people like rats. People don't like to work. If we were left to our own accord, what we would be doing, we would be on a beach somewhere sipping mojitos. and and the only reason we work is because we need to get money so that we can eventually sit on the beach drinking mojitos. But the basic motivation is to enjoy leisure and not work. And everything else is just a distraction for me in order so we we can do that. And it's a fine model, but we should ask ourel is this really a correct depiction of human motivation? Is this really what gets us to to act and to do things? Um and and one challenge you could think about is mountain climbing. If you look at people who've climbed different mountains and the depictions and histories and stories, you would think this is the most miserable thing in the world. People are cold and frostbite. It's hard to breathe. It's difficult. I climbed a little peak in the Himalayas many years ago. And you would think that you would get to the top and you would sit there and enjoy the view. No. It's cold. It's miserable. you're tired, just go down as fast as possible from that point on. And if you think about this behavior and you say to yourself, here is something that every moment seems like agony, right? It just seems like a punishment and then people go down and all they want to do is go up again. They want to recover first, but then they want to go up again. How does this view fit with our notion of people sitting on the beach drinking mojitos? It looks like people are either suckers for punishment, right? we want to punish ourselves or that what really motivates us is not relaxation, it's not comfort, it's other things. It's about achievement, it's about conquering, it's about pursuing some goal, it's about arriving at some peak. I actually became interested in in this topic uh when one of my ex- studentents came to talk to me. His name was David. He left the university a few years earlier and he became a consultant or some banker on Wall Street. and he worked for a big bank and he told me that for a few weeks he worked on a big presentation for a merger that was going to happen. He worked evenings, he worked overtime, he created this beautiful presentation with statistics and graph and description. He was really proud of his work and he really enjoyed it. And then he send it to his boss and his boss said, "David, great job. The merger is canled." And he was just devastated. And and the interesting thing about this is that he said it from a functional perspective. Everything was great. Here he was he did a good job. He enjoyed it while he was doing it. His job his boss appreciated it and he was certain that he would get a raise when the time came but at the same time he couldn't care now and he was working on some other document at that point and just couldn't care to the same to the same degree. Now the question is what what happened to him? what what is it? Everything functional was okay, but something was something was missing. So to look at this, I decided to do a couple of little experiments and the experiments we started with were about building bionicles. So bionicles are little Lego robots with about 40 pieces and you're going to build them. And we got people to come uh to to the student center and we said, "Hey, why don't you build Legos for money? Do you want to build the first one? You can get $3 for it. Do you want after they finished the first one, you said, "Do you want to build another one?" This one you can get 270 for. When they finish this one, do you want another one for 240, 210, 180, and so on a diminishing pay rate. And people basically had to decide when they want to stop, at what time the money they were getting from building Legos was not worth their time. And we did this in one of two conditions. The first one was just like the way I described you now. people build one Lego after another after another after another. And when they finished building all these Legos, when they finished building each of them, we took them and put them under the desk. And we told them that when they finished the whole experiment, we would take them, we would break them back, we put them back in the boxes for the next participant in the experiment. This is what we call the meaningful condition. It's not really big meaning, but you know, we're academics. Little meaning. The The second experiment we call the condition. And in this experiment, people started building one Lego and when they finished it, we took it back from them and we said, "Do you want to build another one?" And if they wanted to build another one, we handed them back the second one. But as they were working on the second one, we were taking apart the first one in front of their eyes, right? And then if they wanted to build the third one, we would give them that one back. So it was a complete recycling. And and we call this a cifific condition after scissors who kind of pushed the rock over the same hill over and over. And you can ask yourself how much of the demotivating aspect of cisphus come from the fact that he pushed the same rock on the same hill versus if it was a different hill every time, right? So, so building something having it destroyed in front of your eyes and building it again seemed kind of a an essential element for being unmotivated. And here's what we got. In a meaningful condition, people build about 11 robot. In the scissors condition, they build seven. We also asked other people didn't participate in the experiment to predict what would people do. How much more would people build in the meaningful condition and the specific condition and people predicted correctly, but they dramatically underestimated the effect. People thought that the difference about one robot, the difference was much much larger. Right? So, so we all understand that meaning is important. we just dramatically underestimate how important this is. And I will tell you that I I recently was I went to give a talk at a big software company and this was a software company where these were a group of people who worked for two years designing a particular product and they thought this was the best product for this company and after two years of working on it the week before I came the CEO of that company canceled the project and I've never seen a group of more demotivated people in my life right and they all told me they felt like they're part of this Lego experiment right they worked for a long time and something was just destroyed in front of them. And I think basically their boss had the same mistake as our prediction experiment where he understood that meaning is probably a little bit important just didn't understand how big it is. And now he had a group of people who are completely demotivated and so and so on. Um now there was another interesting part of this experiment which is if you look at the correlation between how much people love Legos naturally and how much they persisted you would expect that people who love Lego will build a lot and people who don't love Lego will build a little there'll be some individual difference and indeed there was an individual differences in a meaningful condition people who loved Legos build more people who didn't love them didn't build as many in the specific condition the correlation was zero which tells me that we basically choked every inch of enjoyment people had naturally from Legos, right? People come with a natural appreciation for Legos, some people, and we were basically able to crush that. Uh, so the next experiment, we wanted to find out even what smaller differences could could make. So we gave people a sheet of paper with lots of letters on it and we said look for two letters next to each other that are the same. It was a random set and we did the same thing. We paid them more for the first sheet and next less for the next sheet and so on. And we had three conditions. The first condition every time you gave me a sheet if I was the experimentter I would I would ask you to write your name on the top. I would look at it like this. I would sayhuh and I would put it on the on the pile. In the next condition you didn't have to write your name. I would just take the sheet of paper and without looking at it, I would just put it on the big pile of paper. No acknowledgement, just putting it down. In the third condition, if you gave me a sheet of paper, I immediately took it and shredded it. And now the question is how much will people work in those in those three conditions? And what I'm going to show you here is what is the minimum amount of money that people are willing to work for, right? How long did it go? So low amounts of money mean that people enjoy it more. So we got a replication on the first result. In the acknowledge condition when you say uhhuh people were willing to work up to 15 cents per page really low wages. In the shredded condition they wanted twice as much money. And now the question is what happens in the ignored condition? Is the ignored condition like the shredded? Is it like the acknowledge and then somewhere in the middle? It turns out it was very similar to the shredded condition. So if you really want to demotivate people, you know, shredding the work is really good for that. But it turns out it's simply ignoring them get you a big part of the way. In fact, almost. So this was one part of motivation. It's about um being feeling meaning for what you're doing and acknowledged and so on. And we mostly did this by destroying people's motivation. Let's think for a second about the other part is how we can get people to be more motivated, how we can get people to do to do more. And um the idea here came to me after going to IKEA. So I don't know about you, but I like a Kia, but every time I get this furniture, I I find myself that it takes me much longer than I expected to build this. And the instruction seems confusing. I I I often do a step and then have to backtrack. And when I have to guess something, I think I guess wrong more than 50% of the time. Lots of these things. And and the thought is, is it a is it a the result of this? Do I love my furniture more? The fact that I have to build them, that I create them, does that create a particular attachment between me and my furniture? Call this the IKEA effect. And and and some evidence for this uh exists from cake mixes. So when cake mixes came out in the 50s, h to the surprise of people who made up the cake mixes that were not they were not very popular. And the question is why? Pie crust were popular. Um cookies were popular. All kinds of other ready mixes were popular not cakes. And one of the theory was that maybe people did not have to do much for these cakes. Maybe if you take a mix and you pour it into some thing with add some water, pour it to the oven and then make it and somebody says, "What a great cake." You just can't feel good about it, right? So maybe it was the fact that it didn't require as much work that made the cake mixes not as appealing. This was known as the egg theory. And what they did to test it is they took the eggs out of the cake mix. All of a sudden the cake mix was the same. You just had to add eggs and add some milk to it. What happened now? Cake mixes became much more popular. Somehow having to put work into something make it more appealing. So we decided to try this out. So we gave people instructions to do origami. On the top you have the on the top you have a list of what what all the signs mean and then you have a list of instructions of how to do origami. it's not that easy to do. And we asked people to to do it. And what happened? People created stuff that didn't really look like it was supposed to, right? These were not origami experts. Um, but if we looked at how much people valued the origamis, there was some auction and people could bid for it and so on. It turns out that people who did not build the origami thought it wasn't that exciting and people who build the origami thought it was just fantastic. Right? People who build that origami thought it was great. But moreover, people who build the origami when we ask them to predict how much do these other people value this origami, they thought they would value them as much as they do. So what happened is that the people who build origami not only thought it was wonderful, they also thought that other people would view it in their way. Now we had another condition which is again going back to the IKEA. had people who get easy instructions and for some people we hid the top part. So they didn't really have the rule for how this works out and unsurprisingly they they built even worse origamis. They were much uglier. What happened to the evaluations? People who build it thought it was better than people who just evaluated it. But people who got the hard instructions like them even more. All of a sudden they put more into it. It was more difficult, more challenging. They loved it more. And what about the people who evaluated it? They loved it even less because it was objectively uglier. I think we can think about kind of a good metaphor for this as kids. These are my kids, by the way. Um, and imagine that I ask you, how much would you sell me your kids for? Right? Imagine I could erase your memories and your thought and your emotion about your kids. How much money would I need to give you to compensate you for that? That's one thought. And most people in good days would say lots and lots of money. Or imagine or imagine that uh you didn't have kids and you came to some playground and you met some kids and you played with them for a few hours and after a few hours you knew a lot about them and as you said goodbye the parent of their kids said, "You know, by the way, they're for sale if you're interested. And a little bit like the IKEA furniture, it's because they're ours. we put because we put so much effort into them and because it's hard and complex and difficult, the instructions are not clear and so on. So, so what I want to to propose is that you know we have this incredibly simple model of labor motivation is payment. That's basically it. And if you think about what we do in the workplace, that's basically the model we use. But this is not the right model. In fact, if you think about anything that you see in the world, it's very hard to think that this model is a good description of human behavior. It's not described zero, but it's per definitely not a really good description of what happens. In reality, we have lots of other things. We have meaning, feeling of creation, challenges and so on and so forth. And unless we understand those different elements, I don't think we could create the right environment. Now just as one side comment we can take money and we can make it fulfill other motivations. So for example we can get pride and get people to be proud in how much money they get. We can get accomplishment. We can get competition. Money can be a substitute for all of those other motivations. But it doesn't mean that inherently it's about all of those motivations. So human being are complex. to have lots of things that we strive for like in mountain climbings and reducing all of it to just what salary we're getting is just not the right model. And finally, I want to tell you something about Adam Smith versus KL Marx. Adam Smith has the notion about efficiency in the workplace. The notion was that if you take for example the creation of a pin in the old days and you say how what's the efficient way to create a pin? He said if one person creates all the steps to make a pin, it's incredibly inefficient. But if you get 12 people and each of them went make one steps of creating a pin, all of a sudden together there's a huge efficiency in production and the output from the factory could be dramatically higher. And that was the the notion of efficiency and productivity. And KL Marx on the other hand had this notion about alienation of labor. How connected do you feel from it? And if you take the creation of a pin and you make it into 12 steps and each person does one step, how connected do people feel if they're doing the same thing all the time all the day and they never see the progression or creation or the final product on what they're doing? And I and I think that in the in the pre-industrial age, uh, Adam Smith was right. You could get more value out of increased efficiency that you could get from alienation of work. But but we're not at that age. We are now in some kind of knowledge economy for lots of things that we care about. And I think that in the knowledge economy things actually have reversed. If you say let's take a task programming, creating a computer, whatever it is, and break it to lots of little tasks to make everything much more efficient, maybe we would get more efficiency in the Adam Smith kind of kind of world. But would we get the same kind of improveing caring, motivation, meaning? And perhaps what we're doing is we're just doing the wrong the wrong approach. and we take now big task and try to divide them into lot of things. We're actually hurting ourself. So I think that now things are actually reversed. And just as a final comment, I think we can do lots of things to get people to motivate. I think we can do things to get people to motivate to do much more, but at least I think we should try and not replicate the Lego experiments in day-to-day life. At at least we should try not to decrease people's motivation, which is something I fear we're doing way too often. Thank you very much. [Music]
